clue.text: Half of really friendly city

indicators.note: half of says only the front two of the four letters of the synonym for really are kept

parts.note: really means very
friendly means nice

explanation.surface: Someone praises a place as a really friendly city, then trails off halfway.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian lagoon city is an example of a city.

clue.text: Tramp turning over telly, catching A Grand Day Out

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
turning over says the telly abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: TV is the abbreviation for television, telly in British slang

indicators.note: out says the abbreviation for day is removed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tramp switches over the TV and catches the Wallace and Gromit film A Grand Day Out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catching' puts AGRAN inside VT. Tramp is also the setter's own name.
explanation.definitionFit: A vagrant is a homeless wanderer, a synonym of the noun tramp.

clue.text: North American native that is wrong to be upset

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: ie is the abbreviation of id est, that is
a sin is a wrong

explanation.surface: A native of North America says that it is wrong to be upset.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names a US- or Canada-born child of Japanese immigrants, so a native of North America.

clue.text: Cock-up by one in animated series?

definitions.meaning: British slang for a blunder or embarrassing mistake
knitted mouse-like creatures in a British stop-motion children's series

explanation.surface: A blunder by someone working on a cartoon series.
explanation.walkthrough: The Clangers was a British children's TV series of knitted creatures on a small planet; 'cock-up' is British slang for a mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: Dropping a clanger is a British idiom for making a gaffe, and the creatures are members of the series' cast.

clue.text: Shoot right rabbit on fencing

indicators.note: fencing here means enclosing, so the talk word goes round the letter for right

parts.note: to rabbit on is British slang for talking at length, which is to spout

explanation.surface: A hunter is told to fire at a rabbit perched on a fence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoot' reads as a verb about the rabbit, but it is the noun for new growth; 'rabbit on' is British slang for chattering.
explanation.definitionFit: A new plant shoot is a growth bud, a synonym of the noun for fresh growth.

clue.text: Nick Park

definitions.meaning: to nick is British slang for to arrest someone
to park is to stop a vehicle at the side of a road

explanation.surface: The name of the animator, creator of Wallace and Gromit.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Park, the theme's animator, splits into two verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Police pull in a suspect when they arrest them, and a driver pulls in to stop at the kerb.

clue.text: Demands too much with public cuts

parts.note: overt means done in public, open
axes means cuts, as a verb

explanation.surface: A government asks too much while making public spending cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: To overtax is to strain or burden excessively, so it means demanding too much.

clue.text: Great film

definitions.meaning: James Cameron's 1997 film about the sinking liner

explanation.surface: A short verdict on a movie: great film.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means gigantic, and the 1997 disaster movie about the doomed liner shares the name.

clue.text: Wrong trousers cut below hip

indicators.note: below in a down clue puts the trousers word under the hip word

parts.note: in means fashionable, hip

indicators.note: cut says the final letter is removed

parts.note: to trouser money is British slang for pocketing it, to appropriate it

explanation.surface: A tailor's blunder: trousers cut below the hip, recalling The Wrong Trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' is a verb, slang for pocketing; The Wrong Trousers is a Wallace and Gromit film.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unsuitable for the occasion is wrong in the sense of improper.

clue.text: In which soldiers may drop bombs

definitions.meaning: soldiers are fingers of toast dipped into soft-boiled ones at breakfast
in old RAF slang, bombs dropped from aircraft were called by the breakfast word

explanation.surface: A war picture: troops dropping bombs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soldiers' are strips of toast in British homes, dunked into a boiled egg; aircrew slang also uses the word for bombs.
explanation.definitionFit: Toast soldiers are dipped into soft-boiled ones, and wartime airmen used the same plural as slang for bombs.

clue.text: More than one quashing — mental nuns wrestling

indicators.note: wrestling suggests the words grappling and tumbling over each other, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mad nuns grappling with one another must be stopped repeatedly.
explanation.definitionFit: A quashing of a ruling or marriage is a cancellation; the plural phrase asks for several such cancellations.

clue.text: See 16
Picture headless cartoon character in short episode

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
short says the episode word loses its final letter

parts.note: a page can mean an episode or period, as in a page of history

indicators.note: headless says the character's name loses its first letter

parts.note: Tintin is the boy reporter of Hergé's comic strips

explanation.surface: A cartoon figure without a head appears briefly in an episode, as a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A painting is a picture made with paint, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Home time — one shot to capture route

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: to capture says the attempt word holds the next letters inside it

parts.note: a shot is an attempt, a try
in means at home
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone plans to be home on time, with one attempt to capture the right route.
explanation.definitionFit: A travel plan setting out the stops of a journey is the route someone will follow.

clue.text: Due to land, terribly bumpy

indicators.note: terribly suggests the words are badly mangled, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A plane due to land has a terribly bumpy approach.
explanation.definitionFit: Covered in small knobs or lumps, so having a bumpy surface.

clue.text: Director having sex, second pair of smalls discarded

indicators.note: discarded says the pair of letters is thrown away from the joined words

parts.note: taken as written
sec is short for a second of time
smalls here is read as small letter s, so a pair of them is two s letters

explanation.surface: A company director's affair ends with a second pair of underpants thrown aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smalls' looks like British slang for underwear, but it means lower-case s letters; one goes from each of SEX and SEC.
explanation.definitionFit: An exec is informal shorthand for an executive, a company director or manager.

clue.text: Controlling back of Wallace and Gromit in animation

indicators.note: animation suggests lively movement, so the letters are set moving into a new order
back of points to the final letter of the inventor's name

explanation.surface: Someone is controlling the back end of a Wallace and Gromit animated film.
explanation.walkthrough: Wallace and Gromit are Nick Park's claymation inventor and his dog; 'back of' gives E from Wallace.
explanation.definitionFit: Moderating a debate or a force means controlling it or keeping it in check.

clue.text: Money to tie up, fell over time

indicators.note: over in a down clue puts the fell word above the time word

parts.note: a fell is a hill or moor in northern England
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A walker falls over in time, losing money they wanted tied up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fell' is not a fall but a northern English word for upland moor.
explanation.definitionFit: Moorage is the fee paid for berthing a boat, money for tying it up.

clue.text: Fast runner to show off brand

parts.note: to sport a thing is to wear it proudly, to show it off
a brand is a burn mark, a scar

explanation.surface: A sprinter flaunts a sponsor's brand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast runner' suggests an athlete; it is a vehicle that runs fast.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast two-seater motor is a runner in the sense of a vehicle that goes quickly.

clue.text: On models, section in middle sticks out

parts.note: re means on, concerning

indicators.note: in middle says the section letter goes into the centre of the models word

parts.note: models sit for an artist

explanation.surface: On some models, a part in the middle protrudes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sticks out' looks physical; it means holds out against.
explanation.definitionFit: To stick out against something is to hold firm, to withstand it.

clue.text: Expert presenter of art film, that's clear

parts.note: an ace is an expert
the Tate is the London gallery group that shows art

explanation.surface: An expert presenter of an art film makes the point plainly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is London's national art gallery group.
explanation.definitionFit: Cellulose acetate sheet is a transparent plastic film, used for overhead slides.

clue.text: Fine to take off A Close Shave

parts.note: fine means slender, narrow
to take off is to flee, escape

explanation.surface: A fine to be paid for removing a copy of the Wallace and Gromit film A Close Shave.
explanation.walkthrough: A Close Shave is a Wallace and Gromit film title.
explanation.definitionFit: A close shave is an idiom for a near miss, an escape by a whisker.

clue.text: Vegetable with potassium? Cooks boil hard leaves off end

parts.note: K is the chemical symbol for potassium

indicators.note: cooks is read as a verb on the letters, which are prepared into a new order
leaves off end says the last letter of hard is dropped

explanation.surface: A recipe: cook a potassium-rich vegetable, boiling it hard and trimming the leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooks' rearranges BOIL plus HAR, from 'hard' less its end, into OHLRABI.
explanation.definitionFit: This turnip-like brassica with a swollen stem is a kind of vegetable.

clue.text: Primarily Shaun the Sheep dead drunk

indicators.note: primarily says take the initial letters of the next two words

parts.note: a ewe is a female sheep

explanation.surface: Shaun the Sheep, Nick Park's claymation star, is dead drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Stewed is British slang for heavily intoxicated, a synonym of drunk.

clue.text: Fluid piece from René Magritte

indicators.note: piece from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A piece of liquid art by the Belgian surrealist René Magritte.
explanation.definitionFit: An injection of liquid into the bowel; the word is also used for the fluid injected.

clue.text: Late talks for groups of clergymen

parts.note: late means former, past
orates means makes speeches, talks

explanation.surface: Late-night talks are held for gatherings of clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastorate is the body of pastors, so the plural means groups of ministers.

clue.text: Took home wheels for cheese

indicators.note: wheels as a verb means turns round, so the earnings word is read backwards

parts.note: to take home a sum is to make it, as in made fifty pounds

explanation.surface: Someone carried home wheels of cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wheels' looks like the round form of a cheese; it is the turnaround signal.
explanation.definitionFit: This mild Dutch cheese with a red wax rind is an example of a cheese.

clue.text: Stops to collect Oscar with awards

indicators.note: to collect says the stops word gathers the next letters inside it

parts.note: ends means stops, as a verb
O is Oscar in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: An awards ceremony stops so a winner can collect an Oscar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar' and 'awards' suggest a film prize; Oscar is just the letter O, fitting a puzzle themed on Nick Park.
explanation.definitionFit: To endow someone is to bestow or grant them something, as awarding does.
